I have explained the basic steps of DNS resolution and illustrated the process with a flow diagram showing how a URL entered by a user is resolved into an IP address by querying DNS servers in sequence. 

Can you explain why the DNS resolver first checks its cache before asking other DNS servers?
turns.board:
DNS stands for Domain Name System, and its job is to translate domain names into IP addresses.      1.  DNS (Domain Name System)  translates  domain names to IP addresses.  
 When you type a website URL in your browser, your computer asks a DNS resolver to find the IP address for that domain.    2.  When you enter a website URL, your computer  asks a DNS resolver to find the IP.  
 The resolver first checks if it already knows the IP in its cache; if not, it queries other DNS servers.    3.  The resolver checks its cache or queries other  DNS servers if needed.  
 There are different types of DNS servers involved: root servers, Top-Level Domain (TLD) servers, and authoritative servers.    4.  DNS servers include root, TLD, and  authoritative servers.  
 Eventually, the resolver gets the final IP address and returns it to your computer, allowing it to connect to the website.    5.  The final IP address is returned to your  computer for the connection.  
 The process starts when the user enters a URL in their browser.    DNS Resolution Process    User enters URL   
 The DNS resolver receives the request to find the IP address.         DNS Resolver   
 The resolver checks its cache to see if it already knows the IP address.         Cache Check   
 If the IP is cached, it returns the IP address immediately.       If cached     Return IP Address   
 If not cached, the resolver asks the root DNS server for help.       If not cached     Root DNS Server   
 The root server directs the resolver to the appropriate TLD DNS server.         TLD DNS Server   
 The TLD server directs the resolver to the authoritative DNS server for the domain.            Authoritative DNS  Server   
 The authoritative server provides the final IP address for the domain.
